title: An in-memory file system
objectives: Design classes for a small file system with paths, folders and files.

screens.title: What does ls list
screens.prose: A file system is a tree: folders hold names, files hold text. You built trees in `ds` l14 and walked them in l16. Here the root is `/`, and `/a/b/c` holds a file `d.txt`.
screens.question: Tap the names that `ls('/a')` lists.

hints.text: Does `ls` look inside the folders it lists?
It lists only what sits directly inside `a`.
Only `b` is a direct child of `a`. The names `c` and `d.txt` belong deeper down.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. List only the direct children.

byKey.deep: You listed everything below `a`. `ls` shows only the names directly inside.
byKey.self: You tapped `a` itself. `ls('/a')` lists what is inside it.

explain.text: `ls` lists the direct children of a folder and goes no deeper. The names `c` and `d.txt` are children of `b` and `c`.

screens.title: Making every folder
screens.prose: On an empty file system, call `mkdir('/a/b/c')`. Slide through what it creates, one name at a time.

frames.caption: mkdir creates a, b and c

screens.question: How many folders exist afterwards, not counting the root?

hints.text: Does `mkdir` need the parents to exist first?
It makes each missing folder on the way.
The path has three names, and none existed, so three folders are made.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count every name on the path that was missing.

byKey.last: You counted only `c`. `mkdir` also creates the missing parents.
byKey.root: You counted the root. It was there already.

explain.text: `mkdir` here works like `mkdir -p`: it creates each missing folder along the path. One call on an empty system makes three folders.

screens.title: ls of a file
screens.prose: The file `/a/b/c/d.txt` holds `hello`. A folder lists the sorted names inside it. A file is a different case.
screens.question: What does `ls('/a/b/c/d.txt')` return?

options.why: You listed the file's children. A file has none, but `ls` of a file names the file.
That is what `read` returns, the content.
You returned the full path. `ls` returns the name only.

hints.text: What would a shell print for `ls` of a file?
The file's own name.
A file has no children, so `ls` returns a one-element list holding its name.

feedback.correct: A one-element list with the file's name.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. `ls` of a file is a special case.

byKey.b: A file has no children, so the folder rule gives nothing. The file case returns its own name.
byKey.d: The name is the last part of the path only.

explain.text: A folder lists its children and a file lists itself. The name is the last piece of the path, here `d.txt`.

screens.title: Write creates and appends
screens.prose: Nothing exists yet. Then `write('/n/x.txt', 'hello')` runs, and after it `write('/n/x.txt', ' world')`.
screens.question: What does `read('/n/x.txt')` return?

options.why: You replaced the content. `write` appends.
You stopped at the first write. The second one appends.

options.text: An error, because `/n` does not exist
options.why: You expected a failure. `write` creates missing folders, like `mkdir -p`.

hints.text: Does `write` need the folder to exist?
No: it creates the folders and the file.
The first write makes `/n` and `x.txt` with `hello`. The second appends, giving `hello world`.

feedback.correct: `write` creates what is missing and appends.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow the two writes in order.

byKey.b: That would be an overwrite. This `write` adds to the end.
byKey.c: The second write is not lost. It adds to the same file.
byKey.d: Folders are created on the way, so there is no error.

explain.text: The first write creates `/n`, then `x.txt` with `hello`. The second write finds the file and appends, so the content is `hello world`.

screens.title: Four methods
screens.prose: Use one `Node` class. It holds a dict of children and a `content`, which is `None` for a folder. A file's content is its text. One helper walks a path name by name and can create what is missing. Here `write` appends, unlike a real `write`.

params.title: FileSystem, paths start with /
lines: mkdir(path): make every missing folder. No error if it exists.
write(path, text): make missing folders and the file, then append text.
read(path): the content of a file.
ls(path): a folder gives its sorted names. A file gives [its name].
Hidden driver run_fs(ops): rows ('mkdir', path), ('write', path, text), ('ls', path) and ('read', path).

screens.question: Write `FileSystem` with `mkdir`, `write`, `read` and `ls`.

widget.how: Check runs 5 hidden tests. They cover nested folders, the root, a repeated `mkdir` and sorted names.

hints.text: Which method do all four share?
A walk down the path, one name at a time.
Write `_walk(path, create)`. `mkdir` and `write` pass `create=True`. `ls` returns sorted children, or the file's name.

feedback.correct: One walker, and four short methods on top of it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 makes three folders in one call, then writes and appends to a file.
byKey.test-2: Test 2 writes a file directly in the root.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 lists an empty root. Return an empty list.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 makes the same folder twice. The second call does nothing.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 lists folders and files together, sorted by name.

explain.text: The walker keeps `mkdir`, `write`, `read` and `ls` to a few lines each. `write` appends with `(node.content or '') + text`, so a new file starts empty. `ls` checks `content` to tell a file from a folder.

screens.title: The empty name
screens.prose: A walker loops over `path.split('/')` and looks each name up among the children. It does not skip empty names.
screens.question: What happens on `ls('/')`?

options.text: It looks for a child named `''`, finds none and fails.
It stays at the root, because an empty name is no step.
options.why: You skipped the empty names in your head. This walker looks them up.

options.text: It returns the root's children, since `/` is the root.
options.why: That needs a special case for `/`. A plain walk has none.

options.text: It makes a folder called `/` under the root.
options.why: `split` already cut at the slash. The names are two empty strings, not `/`.

hints.text: What does `'/'.split('/')` return?
Two empty strings.
The loop looks up `''` as a child name. The root has no such child.

feedback.correct: `''` is looked up as a child name, and there is none.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Split first, then follow what the loop does.

byKey.b: The walker in the question has no skip, so it does look up the empty name.
byKey.c: The loop has no `/` case. It treats every name alike.
byKey.d: No `/` name exists after the split. Only empty strings remain.

explain.text: Splitting at a slash leaves an empty name before it, and after a trailing one. A walker that looks those up searches for a child called `''`. Skipping empty names makes `/a`, `/a/` and `//a` walk the same way.

screens.title: A folder's size
screens.prose: Files `/logs/a.txt` (`abcd`), `/logs/old/b.txt` (`xy`) and `/logs/c.txt` (`abcdef`). The size of a folder is the total of every file below it.
screens.question: What is `size('/logs')`?

hints.text: Does `old` count?
Everything below `logs` counts, at any depth.
Add every file: $4 + 2 + 6 = 12$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the length of every file under the folder.

byKey.shallow: You skipped the files inside `old`. A folder's size includes its subfolders.
byKey.count: You counted the files. The size adds their lengths.

explain.text: `a.txt` has 4 characters, `c.txt` has 6, and `old` holds `b.txt` with 2. A folder's size is the sum over its children, so `size('/logs')` is $4 + 2 + 6 = 12$.

screens.title: Add size
screens.prose: Extend the class. The starter is the finished stage from the last problem, with `size` as a stub. A file's size is its length; a folder's is the total of its children.

params.title: size(path)
lines: File: the number of characters in its content.
Folder: the total of every file below it.
size('/') is the whole file system.

screens.question: Write `size(path)`, recursively.

widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests. Five are from the last problem. One asks for the size of a folder, a file and the root. The starter passes five of them.

hints.text: What is the size of a file?
The length of its content.
Write a helper `total(node)`: a file returns `len(node.content)`, a folder returns the sum over its children.

feedback.correct: A file is its length. A folder is the sum of its children.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-5: Test 5 asks for the size of `/docs`, `/docs/n`, a file and the root.

explain.text: A file's size ends the recursion, and a folder adds up its children's sizes. The root is a folder too, so `size('/')` totals every file. Old tests still pass because nothing else changed.

screens.title: The walk
screens.prose:
Every method reuses one helper.

```python
node = self.root
for name in path.split('/'):
    if not name:
        continue                  # skip empty names
    if name not in node.children:
        if not create: return None
        node.children[name] = _Node()
    node = node.children[name]
return node
```
screens.question: Put the walk in order. Leave out the line that does not belong.

lines.text: Look the name up among the node's children
If it is missing, create it or stop, as the method needs
Step into the child and go on to the next name
Return the node where the path ends
Look the whole path up as one key in a flat dict
lines.why: A flat dict cannot list a folder without scanning every key. The walk costs one step per name.

hints.text: What must you know before you look a name up?
You must have a name, so split first and skip the empty ones.
Start and split, skip empty names, look up, create or stop, step in, repeat, return the node.

feedback.correct: Split, skip empties, look up, create or stop, step in, return.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each step needs the one before it.

byKey.d1: You looked up the whole path as one key. A flat dict cannot answer `ls` without scanning every key.
byKey.left-out: Seven lines belong. Only the flat dict does not.

explain.text: The walk is the whole design. `mkdir` and `write` call it with `create=True`, `read` and `ls` without. Each public method is a few lines on top of it.

screens.title: The next question
screens.prose: The interviewer asks for more, one feature at a time. Most are one new method on the class you have. Exactly one of these needs the nodes to remember something new.
screens.question: Which one needs a new field on `Node`?

options.why: You added a field. `rm` removes a name from the parent's children, so it is a method.
You added a field. `find` walks the tree as `size` does, so it is a method.
You added a field. `exists` is the walk returning a node or `None`, so it is a method.

hints.text: Which feature needs a node to store something new?
A flag belongs to each file, so each node must hold it.
`rm`, `find` and `exists` use the children dicts that already exist. A flag needs a field.

feedback.correct: A flag lives on each node, so it is a new field.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which one needs a node to remember something.

byKey.b: Removing a name needs no new data. The parent already holds its children.
byKey.c: Searching needs no new data. A recursive walk finds the name.
byKey.d: Existence needs no new data. The walk already returns `None` for a missing path.

explain.text: A read-only flag belongs to each file, so every node needs a field, and `write` must check it. The other three only read or change the dict of children. Say which kind of change it is before you code.

ideas: One `Node` class holds a dict of children and a `content` that is `None` for a folder. A file is a node with text.
A helper walks a path one name at a time. It skips empty names and creates what is missing when asked. Each method is a few lines on top of it.
A recursive size adds the lengths of every file below a node. A new ask is either one new method or a new field on `Node`.

formula.name: Size of a folder
formula.note: A file's size is the length of its content.
